foundations-scope-and-medical-relevance.quote: Biochemistry studies the chemistry of living systems. Molecular abnormalities can explain disease mechanisms and laboratory findings. Mechanistic understanding supports diagnosis, prevention, and rational treatment.

foundations-elements-and-biomolecule-cla.quote: CHNOPS denotes carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulfur. Carbohydrates commonly provide fuel and participate in structure and recognition. Lipids store energy, form membranes, insulate, and generate signaling molecules. Proteins act as enzymes, receptors, transporters, antibodies, and structural elements. Nucleic acids store and express genetic information.

foundations-functional-groups.quote: Hydroxyl groups support polarity and hydrogen bonding. Carboxyl groups can donate protons; amino groups can accept protons. Carbonyl groups occur in aldehydes and ketones. Phosphate groups contribute negative charge and participate in energy and signal transfer. Two oxidized cysteine sulfhydryls can form a disulfide bond.

foundations-bonds-polarity-and-hydrophob.quote: Ionic interactions are attractions between opposite charges. Polar covalent bonds share electrons unequally; nonpolar covalent bonds share them more evenly. Hydrogen bonds are individually weak but collectively important. Disulfide bonds are covalent links between cysteine residues. The hydrophobic effect drives nonpolar groups away from water.

water-compartments-and-major-ions.quote: About two thirds of total body water is intracellular. ECF comprises plasma, interstitial fluid, and small transcellular compartments. Sodium is the major ECF cation; potassium is the major ICF cation. Solute distribution and membrane permeability govern water movement.

water-polarity-solvation-and-amphipathy.quote: Water is a dipole with partial negative charge on oxygen and partial positive charge on hydrogen. Hydrogen bonding explains much of water's solvent behavior. Hydrophilic solutes interact favorably with water; hydrophobic solutes do not. Amphipathic molecules contain both polar and nonpolar regions.

water-ph-and-logarithmic-scale.quote: pH = -log10[H+]. At 25°C, pH + pOH = 14. A fall of one pH unit means a tenfold increase in [H+]. Acidemia and alkalemia refer to measured blood pH, not the underlying process.

water-acids-bases-ka-and-pka.quote: Acid and conjugate base differ by one proton. Ka measures the extent of acid dissociation. pKa = -log10 Ka. Lower pKa means stronger acid. Weak does not mean dilute; it describes incomplete dissociation.

water-henderson-hasselbalch-calculations.quote: pH - pKa = log([A-]/[HA]). pH = pKa gives [A-] = [HA]. Each unit of pH-pKa changes the ratio tenfold. Above pKa the deprotonated form predominates; below pKa the protonated form predominates.

water-titration-buffer-range-and-capacit.quote: At half-equivalence, pH = pKa and buffering is maximal. The useful buffer range is approximately pKa ± 1. The conjugate base consumes added H+. Higher total buffer concentration gives greater capacity at the same pH and ratio.

water-physiological-buffers-and-compensa.quote: Bicarbonate couples blood chemistry to pulmonary CO2 elimination. Phosphate is important intracellularly and in urine. Ionizable protein side chains buffer H+. Deoxyhemoglobin binds H+ more readily than oxyhemoglobin. Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis lowers PaCO2.

ch1-common-structure-and-classification.quote: The R group distinguishes one amino acid from another. Nonpolar side chains favor hydrophobic interactions. Uncharged polar side chains can hydrogen bond. Acidic side chains are usually negative and basic side chains often positive at physiological pH. Proline has a secondary amino group; glycine has two alpha-carbon hydrogens.

ch1-nonpolar-residues-and-hydrophobic-ef.quote: Nonpolar residues usually do not form ionic or hydrogen bonds through their side chains. They pack inside soluble proteins but can face membrane lipids. Hydrophobic clustering stabilizes a protein's three-dimensional structure.

ch1-polar-residues-and-covalent-modifica.quote: Serine, threonine, and tyrosine are common phosphorylation sites. Asparagine and glutamine have polar amide side chains. Two cysteine thiols can oxidize to a disulfide. Disulfides are especially common in extracellular and secreted proteins.

ch1-acidic-basic-and-histidine-chemistry.quote: Aspartate and glutamate are acidic and usually negative. Lysine and arginine are basic and usually positive. Histidine can donate or accept protons near physiological pH. Local electrostatic environment can shift a side-chain pKa.

ch1-stereochemistry-and-glycine.quote: Chiral amino acids occur as D and L enantiomers. Human proteins use L-amino acids. Glycine is achiral. D-amino acids occur in some bacterial cell walls and antibiotics.

ch1-ionization-titration-and-pi.quote: At pI, average net charge is zero. pH below pI gives a net positive charge. pH above pI gives a net negative charge. Titration curves reveal pKa values and buffering regions. Ionizable side chains add extra titration steps.

ch1-aromatic-residues-and-protein-detect.quote: Tryptophan is the strongest common contributor to A280. Tyrosine also absorbs near 280 nm; phenylalanine contributes less. Tyrosine is aromatic yet has a polar hydroxyl group. The xanthoproteic reaction detects aromatic residues by a yellow-to-orange color.

ch2-primary-structure-sequence-and-funct.quote: Primary structure is amino-acid sequence. Sequences are written N terminus to C terminus. The sequence contains the information needed for native folding, although cells often require chaperones. A changed sequence can produce a changed phenotype.

ch2-peptide-bond-chemistry-and-planarity.quote: Peptide formation is a condensation reaction. The peptide C-N bond has partial double-bond character. Restricted rotation makes the peptide unit planar. Most peptide bonds adopt the trans configuration. Denaturation usually does not hydrolyze peptide bonds.

ch2-secondary-structure.quote: An alpha helix has about 3.6 residues per turn and i-to-i+4 backbone hydrogen bonds. Proline often disrupts an alpha helix. Beta sheets are stabilized by backbone hydrogen bonds between extended strands. Beta turns permit compact folding and often contain glycine or proline.

ch2-tertiary-structure-domains-and-stabi.quote: Motifs are recurring combinations of secondary structures. Domains are modular structural and functional units. Hydrophobic burial is a major folding force in aqueous solution. Ionic and hydrogen bonds are sensitive to pH and solvent. Disulfides provide covalent stabilization, especially extracellularly.

ch2-quaternary-structure-and-cooperativi.quote: One polypeptide has no quaternary structure. Two or more interacting polypeptides create quaternary structure. Hydrophobic, ionic, and hydrogen-bond interactions usually dominate subunit association. Hemoglobin is an alpha2beta2 cooperative tetramer.

ch2-folding-and-chaperones.quote: Folding is ordered rather than a random search of all conformations. Hydrophobic collapse helps organize early folding intermediates. Hsp70 protects exposed hydrophobic regions of nascent chains. Chaperonins provide a protected folding chamber. Many chaperone cycles require ATP.

ch2-denaturation-and-renaturation.quote: Denaturation causes loss of native conformation and usually function. Peptide bonds are generally preserved. Hydrophobic exposure can cause precipitation and aggregation. Reversibility depends on sequence, conditions, and avoidance of aggregation.

ch2-misfolding-amyloid-and-prions.quote: Amyloid fibrils are ordered and beta-sheet rich. Alzheimer plaques contain A beta fragments produced from APP. PrPSc promotes conformational conversion of PrPC. Sequence mutation is not required for every misfolding disease.

ch3-heme-and-adult-hemoglobin-architectu.quote: Functional heme oxygen binding requires Fe2+. HbA contains two alpha and two beta chains. Each globin subunit contains one heme. Hemoglobin subunits associate mainly through noncovalent forces.

ch3-myoglobin-versus-hemoglobin.quote: Myoglobin is monomeric and found in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Hemoglobin is tetrameric and found in erythrocytes. Myoglobin has a hyperbolic oxygen-binding curve. Hemoglobin has a sigmoidal oxygen-binding curve.

ch3-cooperativity-tr-and-p50.quote: T state is tense, deoxygenated, and lower affinity. R state is relaxed, oxygenated, and higher affinity. Positive cooperativity creates a sigmoidal curve. Higher P50 means lower oxygen affinity.

ch3-bohr-effect-and-co2-transport.quote: Bohr effect: active tissues promote oxygen unloading

ch3-bpg-and-oxygen-delivery.quote: One 2,3-BPG binds per deoxyhemoglobin tetramer. It binds chiefly between the beta chains. It lowers oxygen affinity and raises P50. Hypoxia and chronic anemia increase its concentration.

ch3-fetal-hemoglobin.quote: HbF composition is alpha2gamma2. HbF binds 2,3-BPG weakly. Weaker BPG binding increases oxygen affinity. HbF predominates before birth and falls after birth.

ch3-carbon-monoxide-and-methemoglobin.quote: CO reduces available sites and left-shifts remaining oxygen binding. Methemoglobin contains Fe3+ rather than Fe2+. Chocolate-brown blood suggests methemoglobinemia. Oxidant drugs such as nitrates or benzocaine can cause acquired methemoglobinemia.

ch3-hba1c-and-chronic-glycemia.quote: Glycation is nonenzymatic and differs from enzyme-directed glycosylation. The extent of HbA1c formation rises with ambient glucose concentration and time. HbA1c reflects roughly the preceding two to three months with greater weighting of recent weeks. Conditions changing erythrocyte lifespan can bias the result.

ch3-sickle-cell-disease.quote: HbS: a primary-structure change causes polymerization

ch3-thalassemia-quantity-versus-quality.quote: Thalassemia is primarily a quantitative globin defect. Beta-thalassemia leaves excess alpha chains that precipitate. Severity depends on how many genes are affected and whether production is reduced or absent. Beta-thalassemia often raises HbA2 and HbF.

ch4-collagen-triple-helix-and-types.quote: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the body. Gly-X-Y repeats permit triple-helix packing. Type I predominates in bone, skin, tendon, and scar. Type II predominates in cartilage and vitreous body. Type III forms reticular fibers; type IV forms basement-membrane networks.

ch4-intracellular-collagen-synthesis.quote: Hydroxylation occurs in rough ER after residues enter the chain. Vitamin C keeps iron in the reduced state needed by hydroxylases. Hydroxyproline stabilizes the triple helix through hydrogen bonding. Propeptides align chains and keep procollagen soluble inside the cell.

ch4-extracellular-collagen-processing.quote: Procollagen cleavage occurs extracellularly. Tropocollagen self-assembles into staggered fibrils. Lysyl oxidase requires copper. Cross-link density increases tensile strength with maturation.

ch4-collagen-degradation-and-remodeling.quote: Collagenases are matrix metalloproteinases. Initial collagenase cleavage enables further proteolysis. MMP activity is regulated by activation and tissue inhibitors. Excess breakdown weakens matrix; excess deposition causes fibrosis.

ch4-collagen-disorders.quote: Scurvy impairs proline and lysine hydroxylation. Osteogenesis imperfecta commonly involves type I collagen. Glycine substitution can disrupt the entire triple helix. Classic EDS often involves type V; vascular EDS involves type III. Dominant-negative chains can damage a multichain collagen molecule.

ch4-elastin-architecture-and-recoil.quote: Elastin provides elasticity rather than high tensile strength. Tropoelastin is the soluble precursor. Fibrillin microfibrils guide elastic-fiber assembly. Desmosine cross-links connect tropoelastin chains. Elastic recoil is crucial in alveoli and large arteries.

ch4-fibrillin-and-alpha1-antitrypsin-dis.quote: Fibrillin-1 mutation causes Marfan syndrome. Alpha1-antitrypsin inhibits neutrophil elastase. Unopposed elastase destroys alveolar walls and recoil. Misfolded Z-variant AAT can accumulate in hepatocytes.

ch5-active-site-specificity-and-induced-.quote: The active site is created by tertiary structure. Specificity can be absolute, group, bond, or stereochemical. Induced fit is conformational adjustment after binding. Catalytic residues need not be adjacent in sequence.

ch5-catalysis-activation-energy-and-equi.quote: Activation energy is the barrier to reaching the transition state. Enzymes lower activation energy. Enzymes do not change reaction delta G. Enzymes do not change the equilibrium constant. Transition-state stabilization is central to catalysis.

ch5-cofactors-coenzymes-and-holoenzymes.quote: Apoenzyme plus required nonprotein component equals holoenzyme. Metal ions such as Zn2+ or Fe2+ can be cofactors. NAD+ is a vitamin-derived coenzyme and cosubstrate. Tightly bound FAD can function as a prosthetic group.

ch5-temperature-and-ph-effects.quote: Rate rises with temperature until structural instability dominates. High heat decreases activity through denaturation. pH controls active-site residue ionization. Extreme pH can disrupt tertiary structure. Pepsin and cytosolic enzymes have different pH optima.

ch5-michaelis-menten-km-vmax.quote: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]). At [S] = Km, v = Vmax/2. Lower Km commonly means higher apparent affinity. At saturation, adding substrate does not raise velocity further. Increasing enzyme concentration increases Vmax.

ch5-lineweaver-burk-interpretation.quote: y-intercept = 1/Vmax. x-intercept = -1/Km. slope = Km/Vmax. Competitive and noncompetitive inhibitors produce different intersection patterns.

ch5-competitive-inhibition.quote: Competitive inhibitor binds the active site. Apparent Km increases. Vmax is unchanged. Increasing substrate can overcome reversible competitive inhibition.

ch5-noncompetitive-and-irreversible-inhi.quote: Pure noncompetitive inhibition decreases Vmax and leaves Km unchanged. Irreversible inhibition permanently reduces active enzyme concentration. Increasing substrate does not restore the original Vmax. Real mixed inhibition can change both Km and Vmax.

ch5-allostery-rate-limiting-steps-and-fe.quote: Allosteric sites are distinct from catalytic sites. Allosteric enzymes often show cooperative sigmoidal kinetics. Regulatory enzymes commonly occur at irreversible pathway-control steps. End-product feedback conserves energy and precursors.

ch5-covalent-zymogen-and-enzyme-amount-r.quote: Kinases add phosphate; phosphatases remove it. Phosphorylation can activate one enzyme and inhibit another. Zymogen activation is proteolytic and irreversible for that molecule. Induction increases enzyme synthesis over hours to days. Multiple regulation modes can act on the same pathway.

ch5-clinical-enzymes-isoenzymes-and-biom.quote: Plasma enzyme elevation can indicate cell injury rather than increased pathway activity in plasma. Isoenzymes differ in sequence, charge, kinetics, or tissue distribution. ALT is relatively useful for hepatocellular injury. Cardiac troponin is the preferred myocardial-injury biomarker. A result must be interpreted with symptoms, timing, and reference intervals.

ch5-phosphorylation-and-enzyme-conformat.quote: Reversible phosphorylation changes the activity of an existing protein. A phosphate group can alter charge interactions and protein conformation. Phosphorylation can activate or inhibit, depending on the enzyme. Protein kinases add phosphate; protein phosphatases remove it.

ch5-clinical-enzyme-tissue-sources-and-c.quote: Creatine kinase is a sensitive biochemical marker of skeletal-muscle injury. CK-MM predominates in skeletal muscle. Serum alkaline phosphatase commonly originates from liver/biliary tissue or bone. Amylase can be detected in urine after renal filtration. Macroamylase is poorly filtered because the complex is large.

ch6-free-energy-coupling.quote: ΔG predicts feasibility, not reaction rate Actual concentrations can change the sign of ΔG Free-energy changes of coupled reactions are additive ATP is kinetically stable but has high phosphate-transfer potential

ch6-electron-transport-chain.quote: ETC is in the inner mitochondrial membrane CoQ and cytochrome c are mobile carriers Complex II is also succinate dehydrogenase O2 accepts electrons at Complex IV

ch6-oxidative-phosphorylation.quote: Proton-motive force is the coupling intermediate Fo conducts protons F1 catalyzes ATP formation ETC blockade prevents maintenance of the gradient

ch6-inhibitors-uncouplers.quote: Inhibitor: electron flow and oxygen consumption fall Uncoupler: oxygen consumption rises while ATP falls UCP1 supports physiologic thermogenesis DNP is a dangerous synthetic uncoupler

ch6-shuttles-ros.quote: Shuttles move reducing equivalents, not NADH itself Malate-aspartate is more energy efficient ROS damage lipids, proteins, and DNA Antioxidant enzymes limit mitochondrial oxidant injury

ch6-redox-cofactors-and-cytochrome-compl.quote: Complex I uses FMN; succinate dehydrogenase/Complex II uses FAD. Complex II transfers electrons to coenzyme Q without pumping protons. Cytochromes a and a3 belong to Complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase. Cytochrome c transfers single electrons between Complexes III and IV. Dehydrogenases transfer reducing equivalents without directly requiring O2 as their acceptor.

ch6-adenine-nucleotide-translocase.quote: Adenine nucleotide translocase is also called the ADP/ATP antiporter. One ADP enters the matrix as one ATP leaves. Atractyloside blocks the adenine nucleotide carrier. Phosphate transport and carnitine-acylcarnitine transport use different proteins.

ch6-cytochrome-c-and-intrinsic-apoptosis.quote: The relevant redistribution is from the intermembrane space into the cytosol. Cytosolic cytochrome c promotes apoptosome assembly with Apaf-1. Caspase activation drives proteolysis in intrinsic apoptosis.

ch6-high-energy-phosphate-transfer.quote: Phosphoenolpyruvate is a high-energy enol phosphate. Phosphocreatine provides a rapidly transferable phosphate reserve. Carbamoyl phosphate contains a high-energy mixed anhydride. Glucose 6-phosphate is the low-energy phosphate ester in this comparison.

ch6-glucose-oxidation-atp-conventions.quote: Direct glycolytic yield: two net ATP per glucose. Two glycolytic NADH: historical maximum six ATP; modern maximum five ATP. Modern complete glucose oxidation: approximately 30–32 ATP. Modern total includes four substrate-level ATP equivalents plus oxidative phosphorylation. Always state the P/O ratio and cytosolic NADH shuttle when comparing totals.

ch7-monosaccharide-stereochemistry.quote: Aldose versus ketose Epimer differs at one chiral center Anomer differs at the anomeric carbon D/L does not specify optical rotation

ch7-glycosidic-reducing-sugars.quote: Free anomeric carbon permits reduction tests Glycosidic linkages are named by alpha/beta and carbon positions Sucrose is nonreducing Benedict reagent detects reducing sugars

ch7-disaccharides-digestion.quote: Lactose = glucose + galactose Sucrose = glucose + fructose Brush-border enzymes finish digestion Lactase is commonly deficient

ch7-monosaccharide-absorption.quote: SGLT1 transports glucose and galactose GLUT5 transports fructose GLUT2 supports basolateral exit Na+/K+-ATPase maintains the driving gradient

ch7-cyclic-sugar-ring-chemistry.quote: Glucopyranose is a cyclic hemiacetal. A pyranose ring has six ring atoms: five C and one O. The ring oxygen forms a C–O–C linkage. The former carbonyl carbon becomes the anomeric carbon.

ch7-storage-and-structural-polysaccharid.quote: Plant glucose storage: starch. Animal glucose storage: glycogen. Amylose: alpha(1→4) bonds without branches. Amylopectin and glycogen: alpha(1→4) chains with alpha(1→6) branches. Cellulose: beta(1→4)-linked glucose; indigestible to human enzymes.

ch14-gags.quote: Most GAGs are highly negatively charged Hydration provides resilience Hyaluronan is unsulfated Keratan sulfate lacks uronic acid

ch14-proteoglycan-glycoprotein.quote: Proteoglycan = core protein plus GAG chains Glycoprotein glycans are shorter and branched Proteoglycans are carbohydrate-rich Both are formed through specific glycosylation pathways

ch14-mucopolysaccharidoses.quote: Both accumulate dermatan and heparan sulfate Hurler is autosomal recessive Hunter is X-linked Corneal clouding favors Hurler

ch15-lipid-classes-fatty-acid-structure.quote: Saturated fatty acids contain no carbon-carbon double bonds Cis double bonds disrupt packing and lower melting point Longer and more saturated chains generally melt at higher temperatures Triacylglycerol is a concentrated hydrophobic energy store Complex lipids include additional phosphate, carbohydrate, or nitrogen-containing groups

ch15-digestion-enzymes.quote: Acid lipases start digestion Pancreatic lipase is the main adult TAG enzyme Colipase anchors lipase at the lipid-water interface TAG digestion yields 2-MAG plus free fatty acids

ch15-bile-emulsification.quote: Bile salts are made in liver and stored in gallbladder Conjugation increases amphipathic behavior Emulsification increases enzyme-accessible area Bile flow is required for fat-soluble vitamin absorption

ch15-micelles-enterocyte.quote: Micelles cross the unstirred water layer Micelles are not endocytosed intact Long-chain lipids are re-esterified Short/medium chains can use portal blood directly

ch15-chylomicrons-malabsorption.quote: ApoB-48 and MTP are required for assembly Chylomicrons travel through lymph ApoC-II activates LPL ApoE supports remnant uptake

ch15-orlistat-and-ezetimibe.quote: Orlistat inhibits gastric and pancreatic lipases. Less TAG digestion means less formation of absorbable fatty acids and 2-monoacylglycerol. Ezetimibe inhibits NPC1L1-mediated intestinal cholesterol uptake. NPC1L1 inhibition is distinct from HMG-CoA reductase inhibition by statins.

ch16-fa-entry-carnitine.quote: Activation forms fatty acyl-CoA CPT-I is the regulated entry step Carnitine carries long-chain acyl groups Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I

ch16-beta-oxidation.quote: Occurs mainly in mitochondrial matrix Four recurring reactions Produces NADH, FADH2, and acetyl-CoA Propionyl-CoA is glucogenic through succinyl-CoA

ch16-tag-lipolysis.quote: Glycerol 3-phosphate supplies the TAG backbone Insulin promotes adipose TAG storage Fasting activates lipolysis Released fatty acids bind albumin Glycerol is handled mainly by liver

ch16-oxidation-disorders.quote: Low glucose plus low ketones suggests FA-oxidation failure MCAD is autosomal recessive Avoid fasting Dicarboxylic acids reflect omega oxidation

ch16-carnitine-amino-acid-origins.quote: Lysine provides carnitine’s carbon skeleton. Methionine, through SAM, supplies methyl groups. Liver and kidney synthesize carnitine; muscle depends on uptake. The carnitine shuttle transfers long-chain acyl groups into mitochondria.

ch16-lipogenesis-carbon-nadph-and-acyl-c.quote: Citrate crosses the inner membrane; acetyl-CoA does not diffuse across it. ATP-citrate lyase produces cytosolic acetyl-CoA. Malic enzyme produces pyruvate, CO2, and NADPH from malate. The ACP phosphopantetheine arm derives from vitamin B5. Citrate activates ACC; malonyl-CoA supplies FAS and inhibits CPT-I.

ch16-fatty-acid-desaturation-limits.quote: The principal site of long-chain fatty-acid desaturation is smooth ER. Delta numbering begins at the carboxyl carbon. Humans lack delta-12 and delta-15 desaturases. Linoleic acid is omega-6; alpha-linolenic acid is omega-3.

ch16-beta-oxidation-stoichiometry-and-at.quote: A standard cycle gives one NADH, one FADH2, and an acetyl-CoA; final cleavage gives two acetyl-CoA. Enoyl-CoA hydratase consumes water. Fatty-acid activation to acyl-CoA costs two ATP equivalents. Modern palmitate calculation: 8 × 10 + 7 × 2.5 + 7 × 1.5 - 2 = 106 ATP. The sixth-edition legacy calculation gives 129 ATP net. A pre-existing double bond can reduce FADH2 production during oxidation.

ch16-odd-chain-oxidation-and-energy-comp.quote: Pentadecanoate (C15:0) yields six acetyl-CoA plus one propionyl-CoA. Propionyl-CoA carboxylase uses biotin and ATP. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase uses adenosylcobalamin (B12). Succinyl-CoA can contribute carbon to gluconeogenesis. Energy accounting depends on whether residual carbon stops at oxaloacetate or is fully oxidized. Even-chain acetyl-CoA cannot give net glucose: PDH is irreversible and the TCA cycle has no net carbon gain.

ch16-adipose-lipase-sequence-and-hormone.quote: ATGL: triacylglycerol to diacylglycerol. HSL preferentially hydrolyzes diacylglycerol. Monoacylglycerol lipase completes glycerol release. Catecholamines promote cAMP/PKA signaling; insulin opposes lipolysis. Plasma nonesterified fatty acids are albumin-bound.

ch16-ketone-identities-and-fasting-signa.quote: Ketone bodies: acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone. Fasting favors ketogenesis through a low insulin-to-glucagon ratio. Acetoacetate is reduced to beta-hydroxybutyrate using NADH. Spontaneous acetoacetate decarboxylation produces acetone. Mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase is the rate-limiting enzyme. Hepatocytes lack thiophorase (SCOT); RBCs lack the mitochondria needed for ketone oxidation.

ch17-phospholipids-signaling.quote: Polar head and hydrophobic tails Phospholipids form bilayers PLC cleaves PIP2 IP3 raises cytosolic Ca2+ DAG activates PKC

ch17-surfactant.quote: DPPC is the major surface-active phospholipid Made by type II pneumocytes Reduces surface tension Deficiency causes neonatal RDS

ch17-sphingolipids.quote: Ceramide is the common sphingolipid core Tay-Sachs: GM2 and hexosaminidase A Niemann-Pick A/B: sphingomyelinase Gaucher: glucocerebrosidase

ch17-eicosanoids-cox.quote: Arachidonic acid, cyclooxygenase products, and NSAIDs

ch17-leukotrienes.quote: 5-LOX produces leukotrienes Leukotrienes are not blocked by NSAIDs Cysteinyl leukotrienes constrict bronchi Montelukast blocks their receptor

ch18-cholesterol-synthesis.quote: Cholesterol synthesis, HMG-CoA reductase, and statins

ch18-bile-acids-elimination.quote: Biliary secretion is the net elimination route 7-alpha-hydroxylase is rate limiting Bile salts are amphipathic Most bile salts are recycled

ch18-apo-lipoprotein-map.quote: ApoB-48: chylomicron structure ApoB-100: VLDL/LDL structure and LDL-receptor ligand ApoC-II activates LPL ApoE clears remnants ApoA-I activates LCAT

ch18-ldl-atherosclerosis.quote: LDL-receptor uptake and atherosclerotic foam cells

ch18-hdl-reverse-transport.quote: ABCA1 loads cholesterol onto apoA-I LCAT esterifies HDL cholesterol SR-B1 supports selective hepatic uptake CETP exchanges HDL cholesteryl ester for TAG

ch18-steroidogenesis.quote: Cholesterol is the common precursor StAR controls mitochondrial entry CYP11A1 makes pregnenolone Steroid receptors regulate transcription

ch18-lipoprotein-lipases-and-receptor-li.quote: LPL hydrolyzes TAG in chylomicrons and VLDL. LPL or apoC-II deficiency causes familial chylomicronemia. Hepatic lipase helps remodel IDL into LDL. LDL-receptor ligands include apoB-100 and apoE. ApoB-48 does not supply the apoB-100 LDL-receptor binding site.

ch18-bile-acid-feedback-and-sequestratio.quote: Bile acids suppress cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase. Terminal-ileal reabsorption maintains the enterohepatic bile-salt pool. Sequestrants prevent intestinal bile-acid reabsorption. Increased conversion of hepatic cholesterol to bile acids helps lower plasma LDL.

ch23-insulin-action.quote: Insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase GLUT4 is in muscle and adipose tissue Insulin promotes storage and synthesis Insulin suppresses hepatic glucose output

ch23-glucagon-counterregulation.quote: Glucagon uses Gs-cAMP-PKA Primary target is liver No direct glucagon-driven muscle glycogenolysis Counterregulation protects against hypoglycemia

ch23-hypoglycemia-recognition-and-diagno.quote: Autonomic symptoms are early warning signs Neuroglycopenia causes confusion, seizures, and coma Ethanol inhibits gluconeogenesis through a high-NADH redox shift C-peptide distinguishes endogenous from injected insulin Interpret insulin and C-peptide only in the context of documented low glucose

ch24-early-fasting.quote: Glycogenolysis dominates first Gluconeogenesis rises with fasting duration Lipolysis supplies fatty acids and glycerol Liver preserves glucose for dependent tissues

ch24-prolonged-fasting.quote: Brain progressively uses ketones Ketones spare muscle protein RBCs cannot use ketones Liver makes but does not consume ketones

ch24-tissue-fuel-exceptions.quote: RBC: glucose only for ATP Liver: produces ketones Brain: glucose, then more ketones in fasting Muscle: flexible fuel use

ch24-muscle-fuel-in-prolonged-starvation.quote: Resting muscle favors fatty acids during prolonged starvation. Late reduction in muscle ketone use helps preserve ketones for the brain. Brain ketone use reduces the need for muscle-protein breakdown. These resting-starvation adaptations do not describe all exercise intensities.

ch25-diabetes-pathophysiology.quote: Type 1: absolute insulin deficiency Type 2: insulin resistance plus beta-cell dysfunction Both cause hyperglycemia Type 1 has greater DKA risk

ch25-diagnosis-monitoring.quote: Repeat abnormal testing when symptoms are absent HbA1c reflects recent months RBC lifespan affects HbA1c Diagnosis and treatment targets are not identical

ch25-dka-hhs.quote: DKA has significant ketonemia and acidosis HHS has more extreme hyperosmolality Osmotic diuresis drives dehydration Potassium balance requires close monitoring

ch25-chronic-complications.quote: AGEs alter proteins and vessels Sorbitol creates osmotic stress Microvascular disease affects retina, kidney, and nerves Cardiovascular risk is increased

ch26-obesity-measures-risk.quote: BMI = kg/m2 BMI 30 or greater conventionally indicates obesity Visceral fat carries higher metabolic risk Interpret BMI in clinical context

ch26-appetite-hormones.quote: Leptin reflects adipose stores Common obesity has leptin resistance Ghrelin stimulates appetite NPY/AgRP neurons are orexigenic

ch26-adipose-endocrine-organ.quote: Adipose tissue secretes adipokines Adiponectin falls in obesity Inflammation promotes insulin resistance Free-fatty-acid flux worsens ectopic lipid storage

ch27-dietary-reference-intakes.quote: EAR covers about half of a group RDA covers nearly all healthy individuals AI substitutes when evidence is insufficient UL addresses toxicity risk

ch27-energy-macronutrients.quote: Fat: 9 kcal/g Alcohol: 7 kcal/g Carbohydrate/protein: 4 kcal/g Basal metabolism is usually the largest component Protein has high thermic effect

ch27-essential-nutrients-nitrogen.quote: Linoleic acid is omega-6 Alpha-linolenic acid is omega-3 Essential amino acids must come from diet Nitrogen balance reflects protein gain or loss

ch27-protein-energy-malnutrition.quote: Kwashiorkor: edema and fatty liver Marasmus: severe wasting Low albumin contributes to edema Infection commonly complicates both

ch28-vitamin-framework.quote: B and C are water soluble A, D, E, and K are fat soluble Coenzymes may be loosely or tightly bound Fat malabsorption threatens A/D/E/K Storage increases toxicity potential

ch28-thiamine.quote: Active form is TPP Required by three major dehydrogenase complexes Required by transketolase Deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff and beriberi

ch28-riboflavin-niacin.quote: B2 gives FMN and FAD B3 gives NAD and NADP NADH favors energy production NADPH favors reductive work Pellagra is niacin deficiency

ch28-b5-b6-biotin.quote: B5 supports acyl transfer PLP supports amino-acid reactions Isoniazid can cause B6 deficiency Biotin supports carboxylation Avidin binds biotin

ch28-folate-b12.quote: Folate supports nucleotide synthesis B12 requires intrinsic factor Both can cause megaloblastic anemia Neurologic deficits and methylmalonate favor B12 deficiency Folate prevents neural-tube defects

ch28-vitamins-a-d.quote: 11-cis-retinal supports vision Retinoic acid controls transcription Vitamin D activation uses skin, liver, kidney Calcitriol increases calcium/phosphate availability A and D can be toxic in excess

ch28-vitamins-e-k-c.quote: Vitamin E protects membranes Vitamin K enables gamma-carboxylation PT rises early in vitamin-K deficiency Vitamin C supports collagen hydroxylation Fat malabsorption threatens E and K

ch28-calcitriol-and-calcium-conservation.quote: Calcitriol is active vitamin D, not a B-vitamin coenzyme. The kidney performs the final activating hydroxylation. Calcitriol increases intestinal calcium uptake and renal calcium reabsorption. Deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

bio-29-nucleotide-chemistry.quote: Nucleoside = base + sugar; nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate. Ribose has a 2′-OH, whereas deoxyribose has 2′-H. A and G are purines; C, T, and U are pyrimidines. The backbone linkage is 3′→5′ phosphodiester, and sequences are written 5′→3′.

bio-29-dna-duplex-and-melting.quote: The strands are complementary and antiparallel. A–T has two hydrogen bonds; G–C has three. Base stacking also makes a major contribution to duplex stability. B-DNA is physiologic and right-handed; Z-DNA is left-handed. Denaturation is strand separation without backbone hydrolysis and can be reversed by controlled annealing.

bio-29-chromatin-nucleosome.quote: Core octamer = 2 × H2A, H2B, H3, and H4. Histones bind negatively charged DNA because they are rich in lysine and arginine. H1 is the linker histone. Open euchromatin is generally more transcriptionally active than compact heterochromatin. Histone-tail modifications can recruit proteins that activate or repress genes.

bio-29-replication-origins.quote: Each parental strand is a template for a complementary daughter strand. An origin opens into a replication bubble with two forks. Bacterial chromosomes usually use one main origin; eukaryotic chromosomes use many. Origin firing is restricted so each segment is copied once per cell cycle.

bio-29-replication-fork-machinery.quote: DnaB is the principal bacterial replicative helicase. SSB prevents reannealing and protects exposed single-stranded DNA. Topoisomerase I changes linking number in steps of one. Topoisomerase II changes linking number in steps of two and includes bacterial DNA gyrase.

bio-29-leading-lagging-synthesis.quote: Polymerase reads template 3′→5′ while synthesizing 5′→3′. A primer supplies the initial paired 3′-OH. Leading synthesis is continuous; lagging synthesis is discontinuous. Okazaki fragments arise from antiparallel template geometry.

bio-29-polymerases-proofreading-ligation.quote: Bacterial DNA polymerase III performs most fork elongation. Proofreading exonuclease is 3′→5′. Bacterial DNA polymerase I removes primers with 5′→3′ exonuclease. DNA ligase seals, but does not fill, a nick. PCNA is the eukaryotic sliding clamp.

bio-29-eukaryotic-polymerases-telomeres.quote: Polymerase α/primase initiates; polymerases ε and δ perform most nuclear elongation. Polymerase γ replicates mitochondrial DNA. Telomerase contains RNA plus telomerase reverse transcriptase. Telomerase is active in germ/stem cells and commonly reactivated in cancer. Progressive telomere shortening contributes to replicative senescence.

bio-29-double-strand-break-repair.quote: HR is template directed and favored in S/G2 when a sister chromatid is available. NHEJ is available more broadly but is intrinsically error prone. BRCA1 and BRCA2 participate in homologous recombination. End-joining errors can create deletions and translocations.

bio-30-rna-types-and-mrna-architecture.quote: mRNA is the translated RNA; tRNA decodes; rRNA forms the catalytic ribosome. RNA uses ribose and uracil and is usually single stranded. Bacterial transcription and translation can be coupled. Eukaryotic pre-mRNA is processed in the nucleus before translation.

bio-30-bacterial-transcription-initiatio.quote: RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA 5′→3′ without a primer. Sigma confers promoter specificity but is not the elongating catalytic core. Canonical bacterial promoter elements are near −35 and −10. Promoter sequences are not themselves transcribed.

bio-30-transcription-elongation-terminat.quote: RNA grows 5′→3′ and the template is read 3′→5′. Coding-strand sequence corresponds to RNA with T replaced by U. Sigma commonly dissociates after promoter clearance. Intrinsic termination requires a hairpin plus a U-rich tract. Rho binds RNA and catches a paused polymerase.

bio-30-eukaryotic-rna-polymerases.quote: Pol I: 45S pre-rRNA → 18S, 5.8S, 28S. Pol II: pre-mRNA and selected sn/miRNAs. Pol III: tRNA and 5S rRNA. Pol I acts in the nucleolus; Pol II and III act in the nucleoplasm.

bio-30-pol2-promoter-general-factors.quote: TATA/Hogness box is a core promoter element near −25 in many genes. TBP is part of TFIID. General factors position Pol II and create an open complex. TFIIH has helicase and kinase activities.

bio-30-cap-polyadenylation.quote: The cap is 7-methylguanosine linked 5′–5′. The cap supports stability, export, and ribosome recruitment. AAUAAA directs cleavage/polyadenylation. Poly(A) polymerase adds the non-templated tail. Histone mRNAs are an important poly(A)-tail exception.

bio-30-splicing-alternative-splicing.quote: Introns are removed and exons are ligated by the spliceosome. The branch-point A forms a 2′–5′ bond in the lariat. Consensus boundaries are usually GU at the 5′ end and AG at the 3′ end. Alternative splicing expands the proteome without adding genes. Splice-site mutations can alter the reading frame or introduce premature stops.

bio-30-transcription-inhibitors.quote: Actinomycin D targets DNA and inhibits transcription broadly. Rifampicin selectively targets bacterial RNA polymerase. α-Amanitin is most potent against Pol II. Selectivity depends on whether the target is DNA itself or a domain-specific polymerase.

bio-31-genetic-code-and-mutations.quote: Degenerate does not mean ambiguous. AUG usually initiates translation and also encodes methionine. UAA, UAG, and UGA are stop codons. Missense changes an amino acid; nonsense creates a stop; frameshift changes downstream codon grouping. Silent substitutions can still affect splicing or translation efficiency.

bio-31-trna-charging-wobble.quote: Each amino acid has a corresponding synthetase specificity system. Charging consumes ATP to AMP, equivalent to two high-energy phosphate bonds. The ribosome checks codon–anticodon pairing but cannot verify the attached amino acid. Wobble explains why fewer tRNAs than sense codons are required.

bio-31-ribosome-sites-direction.quote: A = aminoacyl entry, P = peptidyl chain, E = exit. Protein elongates N→C. Peptide-bond energy comes from the high-energy aminoacyl-tRNA ester bond. Bacterial 23S rRNA is the peptidyl-transferase catalyst.

bio-31-initiation-prokaryote-eukaryote.quote: Shine–Dalgarno is bacterial; Kozak/cap scanning is eukaryotic. Initiator tRNA starts in the P site, not the A site. Bacterial initiation uses fMet-tRNA. Initiation factors and GTP assemble the complete ribosome only after correct start recognition.

bio-31-elongation-cycle.quote: EF-Tu delivers charged tRNA; EF-Ts reloads EF-Tu with GTP. Peptidyl transfer precedes translocation. EF-G is the bacterial translocase. Eukaryotic homologs include eEF1A and eEF2. At least two GTP molecules are hydrolyzed per elongation cycle.

bio-31-termination-polysomes.quote: Stop codons are recognized by release factors, not suppressor tRNAs under normal conditions. Termination hydrolyzes the peptidyl-tRNA ester bond. Ribosomal subunits, mRNA, and tRNA are recycled. A polysome is many ribosomes translating one mRNA.

bio-31-protein-targeting.quote: Signal sequences direct proteins to ER, nucleus, and mitochondria

bio-31-posttranslational-processing-qual.quote: Modification can activate a precursor, target a protein, or change stability. N-linked glycosylation is on Asn; O-linked is commonly on Ser/Thr. Collagen proline/lysine hydroxylation requires vitamin C. Vitamin K supports γ-carboxylation of glutamate in clotting proteins. Polyubiquitin commonly marks proteins for proteasomal degradation.

bio-31-translation-inhibitors-toxins.quote: Tetracycline: blocks A-site entry on bacterial ribosomes. Macrolides: 50S binding and impaired translocation. Chloramphenicol: inhibits bacterial/mitochondrial peptidyl transferase. Puromycin: aminoacyl-tRNA analog causing premature termination. Diphtheria toxin targets eEF2; ricin targets 28S rRNA.

bio-32-regulatory-logic-cis-trans.quote: Cis = local DNA sequence; trans = diffusible regulator. Promoters, operators, enhancers, and response elements are cis elements. Repressors, activators, and many transcription factors act in trans. Operons coordinate related bacterial genes efficiently.

bio-32-lac-operon.quote: Allolactose is the inducer that inactivates lac repressor. Low glucose → high cAMP → active CAP. Lactose present removes negative control; low glucose provides positive control. Maximal lacZYA transcription: lactose present, glucose absent. Glucose-mediated suppression is catabolite repression.

bio-32-trp-operon-attenuation.quote: Lac is inducible and catabolic; trp is repressible and anabolic. Tryptophan activates its repressor as a corepressor. Attenuation depends on coupled transcription and translation. High Trp favors termination; low Trp permits transcription.

bio-32-eukaryotic-combinatorial-control.quote: Enhancers are cis DNA elements; activators are trans proteins. Enhancer action is often distance and orientation independent. Combinatorial control lets a limited factor set specify many expression patterns. Shared consensus elements coordinate unlinked genes.

bio-32-hormonal-gene-regulation.quote: Nuclear receptors are ligand-activated transcription factors. HRE is cis acting; hormone–receptor complex is trans acting. Glucagon → GPCR → cAMP → PKA → CREB → CRE. Coactivator versus corepressor recruitment determines transcriptional direction.

bio-32-epigenetic-chromatin-control.quote: Epigenetic change alters expression without changing base sequence. Histone acetylation commonly opens chromatin. DNA methyltransferases use S-adenosylmethionine as methyl donor. Promoter CpG-island methylation usually represses transcription. Chromatin remodeling repositions or ejects nucleosomes.

bio-32-posttranscriptional-control.quote: One pre-mRNA can yield different isoforms through alternative processing. RNA editing changes transcript information without changing genomic DNA. ApoB-48 is intestinal; ApoB-100 is hepatic. Longer mRNA half-life generally permits more protein synthesis. Iron-response elements provide a classic stability/translation control system.

bio-32-rnai-translation-control.quote: Dicer helps generate short RNA duplexes; Argonaute is the RISC effector. Partial pairing usually represses translation; extensive pairing favors cleavage. siRNA can be experimentally or therapeutically supplied. Phosphorylated eIF2 inhibits translation initiation during stress.

bio-32-genome-rearrangement-copy-number-.quote: Somatic V(D)J recombination permanently rearranges lymphocyte DNA. Copy-number increase can drive overexpression and drug resistance. Transposons use transposase; retrotransposons use an RNA intermediate. Mobile elements can cause insertional mutation or move resistance genes.

bio-33-restriction-cloning.quote: Restriction enzymes cut sequence-specific sites. Compatible sticky ends improve directional assembly efficiency. DNA ligase covalently seals vector and insert. Origin, selectable marker, and cloning site are core vector features.

bio-33-cdna-probes.quote: cDNA reflects the transcripts present in the sampled cell. Mature-mRNA-derived cDNA lacks introns. Reverse transcriptase makes the initial DNA copy. Probe specificity depends on complementarity, temperature, salt, and mismatch tolerance.

bio-33-pcr-rtpcr.quote: Cycle order: denature → anneal → extend. Primers determine specificity and amplicon boundaries. Thermostable polymerase survives repeated heating. RT-PCR begins with reverse transcription of RNA. Quantitative PCR follows amplification using fluorescence.

bio-33-rflp-sanger.quote: RFLP detects sequence-dependent fragment-length differences. ddNTP incorporation prevents the next phosphodiester bond. Sanger products differ by one nucleotide in length. Sequence is read from the order of labeled terminated fragments.

bio-33-expression-arrays-allele-specific.quote: Microarray signal estimates relative mRNA abundance through cDNA. Allele-specific probes depend on mismatch-sensitive stringency. Hybridization results require normalization and suitable controls. Expression change does not prove a causal functional change.

bio-lab-carbohydrate-general-tests.quote: Molisch: general carbohydrate; violet interfacial ring. Iodine: starch/polysaccharide; blue-black complex. Benedict: reducing sugar; colored Cu2O precipitate after heating. A positive broad test does not identify the exact carbohydrate.

bio-lab-carbohydrate-differentiation-tes.quote: Benedict estimates reducing-sugar amount only roughly by color. Barfoed separates rapid monosaccharide reduction from slower disaccharide reduction. Seliwanoff favors rapid ketose detection. Timing matters: prolonged heating can create misleading late positives.

bio-lab-amino-acid-protein-tests.quote: Ninhydrin: free amino groups; purple for most amino acids. Proline is the yellow ninhydrin exception. Biuret: Cu2+ complex with multiple peptide bonds in alkali. Xanthoproteic: aromatic amino-acid residues; yellow-to-orange product.

bio-lab-volumetric-technique.quote: Volumetric pipette: one precise delivered volume. Volumetric flask: one precise contained final volume. Read the lower aqueous meniscus at eye level. Burette: variable controlled delivery for titration. Correct pipette fillers are used; mouth pipetting is never acceptable.

bio-lab-equipment-safety-separation.quote: Fume hood protects from chemical vapors; it does not guarantee product sterility. Analytical balance doors reduce air-current error. Centrifugation separates by sedimentation behavior, not pH alone. Rotors must be balanced by mass and tube position before spinning. Use relative centrifugal force when protocols require cross-instrument reproducibility.

bio-lab-acid-base-titration.quote: Titrant is known; analyte is unknown. Teacher standard: 0.1 N NaOH. Endpoint is persistent pale pink, not deep pink. Normality counts reactive equivalents per liter. Record initial and final burette readings and use their difference.

bio-lab-enzyme-assays.quote: Use initial velocity in the linear range. A blank measures non-analyte/reagent background. Activity depends on temperature, pH, substrate concentration, and assay time. An enzyme unit is a rate under specified conditions, not a mass. Boiling usually destroys activity by denaturing protein structure.

bio-lab-spectrophotometry.quote: A = εbc within the validated linear range. Absorbance is −log10 of fractional transmittance. Blank composition should match the sample except for the measured analyte/reaction. Use λmax for sensitivity. Dilute and apply the dilution factor when absorbance exceeds the calibration range.

bio-lab-dna-extraction.quote: Detergent lyses membranes. EDTA chelates Mg2+/Ca2+ and suppresses nucleases. Protease removes DNA-bound and contaminating proteins. Salt plus cold alcohol precipitates DNA. Avoid vigorous shearing when intact high-molecular-weight DNA is needed.

bio-lab-chromatography.quote: Rf is unitless and lies between zero and one in a valid planar run. Ion exchange separates principally by net charge. Affinity uses specific target–ligand recognition. Size exclusion: large molecules elute before small molecules. Changing pH or ionic strength can alter binding and elution.

bio-lab-flame-photometry.quote: Flame photometry measures emitted light, not absorbance. Emission wavelength identifies the element; intensity relates to concentration. Na+ and K+ are classic analytes. Standards and blanks establish a valid calibration. Never extrapolate far beyond the highest standard.

bio-lab-osmosis-tonicity.quote: Hypotonic → cell swelling/hemolysis. Hypertonic → cell shrinkage/crenation. Isosmotic does not always mean isotonic. Penetrating solutes contribute little to sustained tonicity after equilibration. Water moves toward higher effective osmolarity across a water-permeable membrane.
